analysis.one_liner: Gives patients the right to control and inspect their medical records, with criminal and civil penalties for unauthorized disclosure.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by two senators, the bill got a single committee hearing in February 1998 and died without a vote or markup before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a national right of medical privacy: patients could inspect and copy their own health records, correct them, and require written consent before most disclosures of their health information. It would have covered not just doctors and hospitals but health plans, life insurers, employers, schools, and researchers, backed by a new federal privacy office, civil fines, criminal penalties including prison for selling patient data for commercial gain, and a private right to sue. The bill sat in the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, got one hearing, and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday patients. The bill's own findings say health information is currently accessible to many people who do not need it, often without the patient's knowledge or consent, and that this erosion of confidentiality can make people reluctant to confide in doctors or even seek care. Patients would gain the right to see and copy their records within 15 business days, add supplements or statements of disagreement, require specific written authorization for disclosure, request that sensitive files be segregated, and sue for damages if their records are knowingly or negligently misused.

how_it_helps.text: Patients gain the right to inspect and copy their protected health information, with the covered entity required to respond within 15 business days, and to add supplements or statements of disagreement to their records.

Disclosure of health information would generally require a specific written or authenticated authorization identifying who gets the data and for what purpose, with a minimum-necessary standard and revocation rights; patients could also require that sensitive information be segregated and kept off networked systems.

The bill sets real teeth: criminal penalties of up to $500,000 and 10 years in prison for knowingly disclosing health data for commercial advantage or personal gain, civil fines up to $100,000 for violations that become a general business practice, debarment from federal health programs, and a private right of action with compensatory, liquidated, and punitive damages plus attorney's fees.
A new Office of Health Information Privacy at HHS would receive and investigate complaints, conduct audits, and report to Congress annually on violations and remedial action.

The bill prohibits retaliation against anyone who exercises its rights or reports a possible violation, and it establishes safeguards, records of who accessed electronic records, and an accounting of disclosures kept for at least 7 years.

analysis.who_pays: Health care providers, health plans, health and life insurers, employers, schools and universities, and researchers would bear new compliance duties: privacy notices, security safeguards, authorization tracking, disclosure records, electronic access logs, civil fines, and potential criminal exposure. Some of those compliance costs would likely be passed to patients through premiums and prices, and insurers and employers would lose the ability to freely share, sell, or use patient health data.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden is broad and real: every listed entity must prepare notices, build safeguards, keep 7-year records of disclosures and authorizations, and log electronic access attempts, costs that would flow at least partly into premiums and the price of care.

Restrictions could complicate legitimate work: medical research facilities would be newly subject to federal human-subjects protections, oversight disclosures must be stripped of identifiers, and the bill would terminate HHS's authority to let researchers use identifiable data without written informed consent if the Secretary misses reporting deadlines or concludes consent is needed.

The criminal and civil penalty scheme is aggressive, with individual fines, entity debarment from federal health programs, and doubled penalties for repeat offenses, which industry would argue deters legitimate information sharing for payment and care coordination, even though the bill carves out administrative billing information for claims payment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy rights are strong and enforceable, which is what privacy advocates wanted, and the bill tries to balance them by carving out emergencies, public health reporting, oversight, and court-ordered law enforcement access. The cost side is genuinely heavy: a wide range of entities faces new paperwork, security systems, and penalty exposure, and some friction for research and payment processing is likely. But the bill's central premise, that patients have little control over how their health information is used, is supported by the National Research Council findings it cites, and the enforcement mechanisms are what make the rights real rather than advisory.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, got one hearing in February 1998, and then sat there until the Congress ended with no markup and no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Patrick Leahy introduced the Medical Information Privacy and Security Act in the Senate on November 4, 1997, for himself and Sen. Kennedy.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on the day it was introduced.
The committee held hearings on the bill on February 26, 1998, but that was the last action the bill ever received.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, with the bill still stuck in committee, so it never came to a floor vote.

The bill's own findings note that HIPAA, the 1996 health law, gave Congress a 36-month deadline to enact health privacy legislation; by failing to pass a bill like this one, Congress left that task to regulation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health and life insurers, employers, and other holders of medical data were better off: with no law passed, there was no enforceable federal consent requirement, no private right to sue over misuse of medical records, and no criminal exposure for selling or misusing patient data, leaving the pre-existing patchwork in place and leaving the privacy rules to be written administratively later rather than by this stronger statute.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks when it was read and referred to committee.

for.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill as its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral, Republican-chaired in the 105th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, held one hearing on February 26, 1998, and never reported it out for a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and the bill never reached a floor vote, so the record contains no roll-call showing where the parties stood.

industries.note: Insurers are covered parties that could no longer disclose health information without specific patient authorization, faced civil fines up to $100,000 for patterns of violations, criminal penalties, and debarment from federal health programs for officers convicted of wrongful disclosure. Their interest in the bill ran against patients' new consent rights.

The bill requires disclosure records, electronic access logs, and minimum-necessary limits, and makes selling or using health data for commercial advantage a crime carrying up to $500,000 in fines and 10 years in prison. Businesses that profit from the free flow of identifiable health data lose that market.

Employers are covered parties that could no longer freely receive or share employees' health information, and could not condition employment on an authorization to disclose it. The bill closes off a channel through which employers learn workers' medical details.

Providers take on the heaviest compliance duties, including privacy notices, safeguards, and 7-year disclosure records, but the confidentiality protections also serve their interest in patient trust, which the bill's findings say encourages people to confide in doctors and seek care.

Research facilities using identifiable health information become subject to federal human-subjects protections, and HHS must report on requiring written informed consent, with its authority to use identifiable data without consent terminated if it misses deadlines. Researchers keep access to identifiable data in the near term but face tighter oversight and a possible consent requirement.
